rationale: This historical-geographical archival study (qualitative design using colonial reports, policy documents, and descriptive historical statistics) examines how early-1900s cholera outbreaks under US colonial rule in the Philippines shaped differential access to potable water and spurred state water infrastructure expansion. Among legal/rule mechanisms, coercive sanitary regulation and policing (enforcement_sanctions)—including armed sanitary inspectors, military policing of the Marikina/Pasig river system to prohibit bathing and domestic use, forced closure of shallow wells, quarantines, and cordons sanitaires—is the most central empirical mechanism analyzed, with secondary attention to costly domestic connection charges under the Carriedo Waterworks (fees_tariffs_subsidies) and state utility/irrigation governance under the Irrigation Act of 1912 and waterworks institutionalization (regulatory_model_ownership). On the outcome side, both water potability/quality, dry-season supply adequacy, and fetching burden (effective_access, the primary focal outcome) and physical infrastructure coverage via urban piped/sewer systems, dams, and provincial artesian wells (primary_connection) are co-equally central (multiple).
